issues.title: Requirement below imposes that all the AI agent are "managed" by the organization. Will it be the case?
issues.author: QiufangMa
issues.body:
OBS-4: Multi-Agent Correlation
The framework MUST support logging and trace correlation across distributed multiple agent execution, supporting querying and analysis.
- The following one is important. We have to recognize here that this requirement imposes HOW the AI agent are built (with historical state)

INT-3: Rollback and Recovery
The supervisor must be able to reverse actions already taken by an agent. Can be a single transaction or a coordinated cross-system reversal of an entire multi-agent workflow.

issues.title: Categorize requirements into several major categories
issues.author: QiufangMa
issues.body:
Also consider including the additional requirements raised by Dan:
•	Risk classification for every action.
•	Maximum blast radius: devices, links, services, customers,  and traffic.
•	Rate limits and concurrency controls.
•	Separation between read, propose, validate, approve and execute roles.
•	Change ownership and locking when agents and humans operate concurrently.
•	Cancellation semantics for queued, running and already completed actions.
•	Defined failure behavior when ICON itself is unreachable.
•	High availability and geographic isolation of the management plane.
•	Reconciliation between intended state and actual network state.
•	An authoritative clock and event-ordering model.
•	Backpressure, sampling and retention for high-volume traces.
•	Privacy classification and redaction for prompts, topology and customer data.
•	Software-supply-chain identity for models, prompts, tools and skills.
•	Protection against an agent falsifying or omitting its own telemetry.
•	Detection of an observability collector losing data.
•	Cross-domain policy conflict resolution.
•	Deterministic precedence between human, supervisor, orchestrator and agents.

issues.title: Toerless‘ review on draft-mcw-opsawg-icon-requirements
issues.author: billwuqin
issues.body:
[ainetops] draft-mcw-opsawg-icon-requirements comments
Toerless Eckert <tte@cs.fau.de> Thu, 08 October 2026 02:37 UTC[Show header](https://mailarchive.ietf.org/arch/browse/ainetops/#)

Dear authors, ainetops:

Thanks a lot for the draft. It is great food for though. Let me provide
some open-ended high-level feedback here . I hope ainetops is a good place
for such discussions. Not sure if there is a better one.

In summary, i think i would like to see more concrete, maybe "lower layer",
"workflow" based text to support or improve  the presented architecture. 

"Bottoms up", aka: let's think about concrete workflow cases, describe them and
derive the guiding architectural principles from those explicitly well
understood work flows. 

Three specific text sections that caught my attention:

>    Existing mechanisms for agent assurance typically rely on static
>    guardrails (e.g., input/output validation, operation allowlists/
>    blocklists, pre-action approval), while assuming that all agent
>    failure modes can be predefined.  Unlike deterministic software
>    systems, however, LLM-based agents exhibit emergent behaviors that
>    cannot be fully anticipated or encoded in static rules.

>    When agentic
>    systems produce novel actions or reasoning paths that fall outside
>    predefined static boundaries, it might lead to risks such as
>    unintended configuration changes, policy violations, or cascading
>    failures in the network.

This sounds nice, but i am not sure it is true: All the problems

"unintended configuration changes, policy violations, or cascading failures in the network."

already exist for even the most simple configuration agents when they are
not programmed to perfection to avoid bugs in provisioning.

When i was younger (oh, here we go... ;-) working with large operators in
service deployment, we had cases where we had to write 100 page long documents
detailling the behavior, especially bad-behavior of specific network service
features under eve non-malicious misconfiguration and possible configuration
guardrails to minimize possible problems impacts.

In other cases, i remember from as much as 15 years ago cases where i
think google reported in blogs problems with competing network automation tools
that lead to misconfigurations making mayor services unavailable for hours.
And other OTT had and maybe still have similar incidents. Long before LLM.

Meaning: Network device configuration is highly fragile and especially older
network operators with institutional memory should be able to tell you that
operations has evolved from something that could be called "cowboy mentality"
- "shoot/configure first, ask questions later" to one of overwhelming
bureaucractic complexity to ensure only network-wide well-known-to-be-problem-free
configuration ever gets committed to network devices.

So, maybe there could be some very concrete examples trying to support
the case the text tries to make.

The only problem i can think of is if AI agents are meant to apply
the good old cowboy mentality again: There is no explicitly coded
deterministic layer to produce bullet-proof configuration from service
intent, but an AI agent - like a lead network operations/architect human
20 years ago just goes along and configures whatever He/She/It thinks is
best. 

In draft-eckert-anima-ai4an, i explicitly tried to point to what i think
is the likely better/safer approach then such "cowboy mentality" (of
back then human operators, no AI agents - shooting off config changes
whenever they think it is helpful), and that explicitly is to let AI agents
do the coding of deterministic code, and that deterministic code can then
be tested up to the wahzoo, like any code is that configures networks.

Most likely you want some AI agents totally independent from the coding agent
to do the validation/testing of the resulting code and possible network
configurations from such code.

Maybe in other words: It is very hard to have an opinion at this
high level of statements without assuming a particular type of
architecture in which the AI agents are operating to get their job done.
such as the spectrum from programming deterministic provisioning code
all the way down to AI agents acting as direct configuration cowbows
for 'whatever CLI config they want to change'.

>    Existing telemetry mechanisms are excellent for tracking traditional
>    network infrastructure or software which are built for deterministic
>    systems.  However, as analyzed in [I-D.wnd-opsawg-icon-ps], they are
>    facing severe limitations when applied to AI agents.  For example,
>    existing logging practices only record what action was taken,
>    completely missing why it was taken, including the agent's internal
>    reasoning provenance and confidence scores.  Existing tracing
>    mechanism designed for static and linear execution path also cannot
>    capture the complex and dynamic execution trajectories of AI agents.

I would split out this whole issue from the rest. First of all, i
think in itself it's not unique to NMA (Network Managmeent Agents) but
a generic issue for all agents, so we should also be able to pull
in a lot of solutions from other domains. It is also i think primarily
a development issue, aka: when the agent is trained for a job, not
only when it is later doing the job.

That's not to say that it's not extremely important to do this. Creating
independently verifyable reasoning traces is definitely a key tool we
need, but i really can only think of simple trace to improve erroneous but
non-malicious behavior of an AI agent. And having grown up with T2
(https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0103064/) i am also worried about actually
malicious AI agents. And unless we figure out how to instrument them
from the outside deterministically, i wouldn't want to trust any
trace data they send me...

>    Existing AI guardrails primarily operate at static boundaries, such
>    as input/output validation and pre-action checks.  These mechanisms
>    are designed to constrain AI agents within predefined operational and
>    compliance boundaries, but they assume that all possible violations
>    can be anticipated and encoded in static rules.  As AI systems
>    increasingly operate in non-deterministic environments, these static
>    measures are proving insufficient as they cannot detect, interrupt,
>    and recover from unanticipated behaviors.

From my understanding, most network operators that employ agentic mechanisms
do not even use them to dare change anything in their running network, but
instead only to observe and analyze what happens - and report to humans.
And the beauty of AI in that workflow is that its done very often completely
without deeper operator insight into what the AI is doing. It's simply
based on the AI recognizing common pattern versus uncommon patterns.
and then ongoing training/refinement when uncommon patterns are encountered.

Arguably, the very same approach can also be taken when looking at
con figuration/operation changes applied to network equipment. And
hopefully it can be done upfront, e.g.: as a checkpoint step. If it
looks uncommon it may be blocked for human approval.

> 
> 4.  Architectural Framework for ICON
(and text describing it)

I have a hard time following the components proposed at the level of
abstraction given. I think it would be extremely helpful to explain
each of the points made with at least one more concrete example,
detailling specifically what novel aspect of control/correct is
needed because an agent is not a deterministically written configuration
agent, but an agentic agent - and whether/how we really assume that
the agent has no deterministic code between itself and the router 
configuration.

Maybe it would also helpful to draw out a likely somewhat lower level
of this architectural framework to better understand the workflows.

For example, high-level i think we need to treat AI agents that result
in change of network configuration just as one may want to treat
human employees doing the same. Especially when they are potentially
evil or much more likely: stupid - oops: cheap and hence unexperienced.
Or with cowboy mentality.

Meaning: Ultimately all output/actions from AI agents hacve to go
through some deterministic intermediary, call it an MCP gateway.
That MCP gateway shouldn't only get what the intended action is,
such as a set of CLI/YANG model changes on network devices, but it
should also get all the bureaucratic paperwork (metadata) required
to allow for this to be done. Something like the credentials of
an agent to perform specific tasks, and all the references needed
for the task, such as "upgrade speed of VPN for customer FOO-INDUSTRIES".

That way, one can instrument the deterministic MCP gateways potentially
with other AI agents to authorize/validate/trace any actions taken
by the AI agent that's authorized to change network config - in
very specific ways. Depending on the task at hand.

Likewise, Input into an AI agent could equally go through an MCP
gateway that performs equally validations against that input. Such
that one couldn't simply abuse an agent with instructions like
"make it look like a valid VPN change to FOO-INDUSTRIES, but
leak routes into EVIL-INDUSTRIES so they can espionage FOO-INDUSTRIES".

In other words: Free text input into AI agents without limits
is something i would at this point in history never have into
an agent allowed to change network config. I would only want it
into AI agents that do analysis. And even then i would still want
to think hard about any additional active diagnostic events such
agents are allowed to do into the network - as opposed to just
looking at post-mortem data outside the network.

Meaning: It would be quite prudent to think of and architecturally
differentiate between those classes of agents: post-mortem
analysis. Active/troubleshooting analysis and actual network
config change. And that's maybe just the start of it.

Sorry if this is overall more text/desire for improvoement/changes
than you'd be interested in, or if it's too low-level. But i just
always feel more confident going bottom up from workflows i do
understand than the high-level architectural representation that
the whole solution might have in the end...
